"Aunty Elizabeth's going to sing that song again," Baljeet groaned, flopping on the bed while the cousins set up for Nani's birthday. "The one that sounds like a sad goat."
"It's a Welsh lullaby," said his cousin Simran. "She sang it at the wedding, at Lohri, at Diwali…"
"Exactly. Every. Single. Time."
That night, in the crowded living room, Aunty Elizabeth sang with her eyes closed. Baljeet mouthed the words before he could stop himself.
Simran nudged him. "You know it!"
"No I don't."
"You're humming, Baljeet."
He was. Later, brushing his teeth, he hummed it again, slower. It didn't sound like a goat any more. It sounded like Nani's house.

qa.q: Where had Aunty Elizabeth sung the song before?
qa.a: At the wedding, at Lohri, at Diwali.

qa.q: What does Baljeet's humming while brushing his teeth suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Baljeet has quietly come to like the song, even after calling it a sad goat. 🙂

qa.q: When Simran caught him humming, Baljeet denied it. What could Baljeet say instead next time?
qa.a: Baljeet could admit the song has grown on him, and maybe ask Aunty Elizabeth what the words mean.

qa.q: How might Aunty Elizabeth feel if she noticed Baljeet mouthing the words?
qa.a: Aunty Elizabeth would probably feel touched and welcome, seeing her song become part of the family's gatherings.

grounding: A boy who mocked his aunt's song finds himself humming it after hearing it at many family functions.

passage: I'm Vikas, and when I was eight I thought the song Deepak Chacha played at every family function was the worst thing ever. It was a slow old film song with a long, wobbly violin bit, and the singer held the notes forever. At Bua's wedding I put my fingers in my ears. At my cousin's mundan, I groaned. At Dadi's birthday I rolled my eyes so hard Mummy pinched me. But by the fourth or fifth time, something changed. I started waiting for the violin part. Then one day at school I caught myself whistling it in the lunch line. Now, whenever I hear it, I think of samosas and cousins.

qa.q: What did Vikas do at Bua's wedding when the song played?
qa.a: Vikas put fingers in the ears.

qa.q: How did Vikas's feelings about the song change, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vikas went from feeling annoyed by the song to happily looking forward to it, shown by waiting for the violin part and whistling it at school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vikas's feelings, and what does it suggest for the next strange song Vikas hears?
qa.a: Around the fourth or fifth hearing, Vikas began waiting for the violin part; next time, Vikas could give a strange song a few more listens before deciding.

qa.q: How might Deepak Chacha feel hearing Vikas whistle the song?
qa.a: Deepak Chacha would probably be delighted, since the song finally reached a child who once groaned at it.

grounding: A child who disliked an old song at family functions grows to love it through repeated hearing.

Sunday

Dear Diary,
Today was Chhote Mamaji's housewarming and the uncles played THE song again. The Punjabi one with the dhol that goes dum-dum-DUM and the man shouting "Hoi!" in the middle. The first time I heard it, at Neelu Didi's wedding, I thought it was just noise. At Mamaji's birthday I covered my ears. At Diwali I made a face at Nazia.
But today, when the dhol started, my foot started tapping by itself. I didn't even decide. Then I shouted "Hoi!" with the uncles and Nazia stared at me.
Now it's stuck in my head and I'm humming it in bed. I think I actually like it. How did that happen?
Shreya

qa.q: What does the man shout in the middle of the song?
qa.a: He shouts "Hoi!"

qa.q: How does Shreya feel about the song now, compared with the first time?
qa.a: Shreya went from thinking it was just noise to liking it, and is puzzled about how that happened.

qa.q: What could Shreya try with another song that sounds strange at first?
qa.a: Shreya could listen to it a few more times before deciding, since this song only grew on Shreya after several hearings.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Shreya shouting "Hoi!" with the uncles?
qa.a: Nazia might be surprised and amused, since Nazia saw Shreya making faces at the same song at Diwali.

grounding: A child who found a family-function song odd comes to love it after hearing it many times.

passage: Every wedding in Kherwadi had the same brass band, and the band had one favourite tune: loud, wobbly trumpets that sounded, Devika thought, like buffaloes arguing. At her cousin Manjula's wedding in Magh, Devika, ten, pressed her hands over her ears and stayed near the cooking fires. At the potter's son's wedding a month later, she rolled her eyes when the trumpets began. At the sarpanch's niece's wedding, she found herself standing at the edge of the crowd, watching the dancers. And at the fourth wedding, in Phalgun, when the band struck up by the temple steps, Devika was in the middle of the dancing girls, spinning with her arms up. Manjula, back visiting, laughed and caught her hand. "Buffaloes arguing, hmm?" Devika spun away, grinning.

qa.q: What did Devika think the band's tune sounded like at first?
qa.a: She thought it sounded like buffaloes arguing.

qa.q: How can you tell Devika's feelings about the tune changed?
qa.a: She went from annoyed, covering her ears, to so happy by the fourth wedding that she danced in the middle of the crowd, grinning.

qa.q: What might Devika learn about judging a new tune after one hearing?
qa.a: That her first reaction may change; hearing something a few times can turn dislike into liking.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula to see Devika dancing to the same tune?
qa.a: Manjula finds it funny and fond, teasing her with her own old words about arguing buffaloes.

grounding: A child who found a wedding tune odd grows to love it after hearing it at wedding after wedding.

The community hall near Karthik's house hosted every family function: weddings, naming ceremonies, anniversaries. And at every one, the band played the same old folk song with a strange, wailing flute.
The first time, Karthik covered his ears. "It sounds like a sad goat," he whispered to his cousin Keerthana. She giggled.
By the fourth function, he found himself tapping his foot. By the sixth, he knew when the flute would rise.
At his aunt's wedding in December, the band began, and Karthik jumped up. "It's my song!" he shouted, dragging Keerthana to dance.
Keerthana stared at him. "The sad goat song?"
Karthik shrugged, grinning. He couldn't explain it. He'd just heard it so many times that now it felt like his.

qa.q: What did Karthik first say the song sounded like?
qa.a: He said, "It sounds like a sad goat."

qa.q: Why does Karthik now call it "my song"?
qa.a: He feels happy and fond of it, because hearing it at so many functions made the odd tune feel familiar and his own.

qa.q: What could Karthik try with a new song he dislikes?
qa.a: He could give it a few more listens before deciding, since songs sometimes grow on us with repeated hearing.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Karthik's change of mind?
qa.a: Keerthana seems surprised and amused, remembering how he mocked the song at first.

grounding: A child who first found a folk song odd comes to love it after hearing it many times at family functions.

Jasleen, you keep asking why I play that old song every Sunday. Sit with your Nani Maria, and I'll tell you.
When I was nine, in Goa, every christening and every wedding in our family had the same song. An old mando, slow and strange. The first time I heard it I thought it was boring, like something for old people. I made faces at my cousins.
But it came again at my cousin's christening. And at my uncle's wedding. And at Christmas. By the fifth time, I knew all the words without trying. By the tenth, I asked my mother to sing it at bedtime.
Nobody told me to like it. It just kept coming, and one day it was part of me.

qa.q: Where did young Maria live when she was nine?
qa.a: She lived in Goa.

qa.q: What was young Maria feeling by the time she asked for the song at bedtime?
qa.a: She felt fond of it and comforted, after hearing it again and again at family events.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how young Maria felt about the song?
qa.a: The turning point came as the song kept returning at christenings, weddings and Christmas, until she knew the words and asked for it at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Maria's cousins have seen her change?
qa.a: Her cousins may have been surprised or amused, having seen her make faces at the song at first.

grounding: A girl who found a family song boring comes to love it after hearing it at many family functions.

Music teacher's note, Class 5, Christmas term

Minakshi's change this month has been lovely to watch. When I first played the Konkani carol for the school concert, she wrinkled her nose and whispered to Tarun, 'It sounds like a sad goat.' Tarun giggled. We rehearsed it every day for three weeks. By the second week she was mouthing the words. On Friday I found her humming it by the water tap, and at the concert she asked to stand in the front row. Afterwards she told me, 'I don't know why, but now I love it.' I will let her help pick next term's new songs, and remind the class that a tune can grow on you if you give it time.

Joan, music teacher
